questions.text: How is the market demand for a good constructed from individual demands at a fixed price?

options.a: Add the quantities demanded by all consumers at that price.
options.b: Multiply one consumer's demand by total income regardless of heterogeneity.
options.c: Average the prices every individual is willing to pay.

questions.text: What is meant by horizontal summation of individual demand curves?

options.a: Incomes are averaged before finding price.
options.c: Quantities demanded are added at each common price.
options.d: Prices paid are added at each common quantity.

questions.text: Market demand generally depends on what besides prices?

options.a: The distribution of income across consumers.
options.d: Only total income, without any assumptions.

questions.text: When does a representative-consumer aggregate demand depend on total income rather than its distribution?

options.a: When aggregation assumptions justify representing market demand with a single consumer's income aggregate.
options.b: Only when all firms are monopolists.
options.c: For every set of individual preferences automatically.
options.d: Only when no prices are observed.

questions.text: What does an inverse market demand function P(Q) represent?

options.a: The total cost of producing Q units.
options.b: The price elasticity of supply at every price.
options.c: The price at which consumers collectively demand quantity Q.
options.d: The income elasticity at quantity Q.

questions.text: Why might the slope of market demand change at a given price even if each individual's demand is linear?

options.a: Some consumers enter or leave the market as price crosses their choke price.
options.c: Individual demands necessarily have a constant elasticity.
options.d: Every consumer must have identical choke prices.

questions.text: If two individuals have demand q1(p) and q2(p), what is market demand at p?

options.d: max(0,q1(p)) + max(0,q2(p)) when negative quantities are infeasible.

questions.text: What is own-price elasticity of demand?

options.a: The absolute price change divided by total revenue.
options.b: The total cost of producing another unit.
options.c: The percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in its price.
options.d: The percentage change in income divided by quantity.

questions.text: For a differentiable demand function q(p), which expression gives point elasticity?
Why is ordinary own-price demand elasticity typically negative?

options.a: Marginal revenue must always be negative.
options.b: Higher own prices generally reduce quantity demanded.
options.c: Higher own prices raise all consumers' incomes.
options.d: Quantity demanded never reacts to prices.

questions.text: When is demand elastic by the conventional absolute-value criterion?

options.b: Absolute price elasticity is less than one.

questions.text: When is demand unit elastic?

options.a: The income elasticity is always zero.
options.b: The absolute value of own-price elasticity equals one.
options.d: The slope of the demand curve equals one.

questions.text: Why does elasticity differ from the slope of demand?

options.a: The slope is always constant for all demands.
options.b: Elasticity normalizes the quantity response by the price and quantity levels.
options.c: Elasticity measures only changes in supply.
options.d: Elasticity has the same units as price.

questions.text: For a downward-sloping linear demand, where is demand most price elastic in absolute value?

options.a: Only at the point where price is zero.

questions.text: For a downward-sloping linear demand, what is elasticity at the quantity-axis intercept where price is zero?
For a linear demand curve, where is own-price elasticity equal to minus one?

options.a: At the midpoint between the two intercepts.

questions.text: What is total revenue as a function of the good's price?

options.b: Price multiplied by quantity demanded at that price.

questions.text: If demand is inelastic and price rises slightly, what happens to total revenue?
If demand is elastic and price rises slightly, what happens to total revenue?
If demand is unit elastic, what is the marginal effect of a small price change on total revenue?

options.d: Equal to the change in marginal cost.

questions.text: If demand is elastic, what is the sign of marginal revenue as quantity expands along a standard downward-sloping demand curve?
If demand is inelastic, what is the sign of marginal revenue as quantity expands?
If demand is unit elastic at a point, what is marginal revenue there?
Why would a profit-maximizing price setter with nonnegative marginal cost avoid an inelastic segment of demand?

options.a: Marginal revenue is always positive there.
options.c: Reducing output would increase revenue and weakly reduce cost.
options.d: Increasing output would increase both price and revenue.

questions.text: For inverse demand P(Q)=a-bQ with b positive, what is marginal revenue?
How does the linear marginal revenue curve compare with linear inverse demand?

options.a: Marginal revenue always lies above demand.
options.b: They have identical slopes and intercepts.
options.c: They share a price-axis intercept, but marginal revenue declines twice as steeply.
options.d: Marginal revenue is horizontal at all quantities.

questions.text: At what quantity is revenue maximized for inverse demand P(Q)=a-bQ?
Which demand function has constant own-price elasticity epsilon?

options.a: q(p)=A-bp with b positive in all cases.
options.b: q(p)=A/p plus a fixed positive amount in all cases.

questions.text: If q(p)=A p^epsilon, what is the slope in a log-log plot of quantity against price?
Which demand specification is unit elastic at every positive price?
For a demand curve that is unit elastic everywhere, how does total revenue change with price?

options.b: It is zero at every price.

questions.text: For constant absolute elasticity greater than one, what is true of MR relative to price?

options.d: MR is positive but strictly below price.

questions.text: For constant absolute elasticity smaller than one, what is true of marginal revenue?
What is the income elasticity of demand?

options.a: The percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in income.
options.b: The percentage price change divided by quantity.
options.c: Market revenue divided by total income.
options.d: The derivative of profits with respect to wages.

questions.text: For a normal good, the income elasticity of demand is what?
For an inferior good, income elasticity is what?
For a luxury good under the slides' classification, what is generally true of income elasticity?
What does an income elasticity between zero and one describe?

options.b: A normal necessity whose demand increases less than proportionally with income.

questions.text: What is the expenditure-share-weighted average of income elasticities across all goods in a fully spent budget?

options.b: The price elasticity of market demand.

questions.text: Why must the expenditure-share-weighted income elasticities sum to one?

options.a: Income effects cancel for every consumer.
options.b: Total consumer expenditure equals income, so expenditure changes add up to the income change.
options.c: Every good has unit income elasticity.

questions.text: If one good in a two-good economy has income elasticity greater than one and both goods have positive expenditure shares, what must be true of the other good?

options.a: Its own-price elasticity must be positive.
options.b: Its income elasticity is less than one.
options.c: It must have exactly zero demand.
options.d: Its income elasticity must also exceed one.

questions.text: What does the Laffer curve relate?

options.a: The market wage to productivity only.
options.b: The interest rate to the present value of income.
options.c: The tax rate to the revenue collected from that tax.
options.d: The quantity of a good to its marginal utility.

questions.text: Why may tax revenue decline when the tax rate becomes very high?

options.a: The taxed activity or tax base can shrink enough to outweigh the higher rate.
options.b: Marginal tax revenue necessarily equals the tax rate.
options.c: Government revenue is unrelated to economic behavior.
options.d: Every higher tax rate always raises labor supply.

questions.text: In the stylized Laffer diagram where no labor is supplied at a 100% tax rate, what is tax revenue at that rate?
If a wage tax rises and labor supply is responsive to the net wage, what force can reduce the tax base?

options.a: A reduction in the gross wage paid by firms to zero in every case.
options.b: A decline in labor supplied as the after-tax wage falls.
options.c: A rise in the after-tax wage.

questions.text: What cannot be inferred merely from the existence of a hump-shaped Laffer curve?

options.a: That some rates can produce more revenue than others.
options.b: That a particular tax cut necessarily increases current tax revenue.
options.c: That tax revenue depends on both the rate and tax base.

questions.text: Along the depicted linear demand curve, which region is most price elastic in absolute value?

options.c: The low-price, high-quantity portion near the horizontal quantity intercept.
options.d: The high-price, low-quantity portion near the vertical price intercept.
